newsitem.title: UK: All change as Major gets used to opposition bench.
newsitem.headline: All change as Major gets used to opposition bench.

text.p: Seconds after Tony Blair ended his maiden House of Commons speech as British prime minister on Wednesday, his predecessor John Major found himself all alone on the opposition front bench.
His isolation on the green leather banquette spoke volumes of the political revolution triggered by Blair's landslide election victory on May 1.
With Blair's speech over, none of Major's senior colleagues wanted to wait to listen to Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown speak on Labour's legislative programme.
None of them felt an obligation any longer to keep Major company and make the Conservative benches, already decimated by the voters, look a little less threadbare.

But Major, as Conservative leader for a few more weeks, had no choice but to stay, blinking unfamiliarly into the sunlight that streams down from parliament's tall windows onto the opposition benches.
After 18 years as a member of Britain's ruling party, Major has never had to squint into that sunshine until now.
It was that sort of day in the House of Commons as members of all parties gingerly accustomed themselves to the unaccustomed.
Blair, in a low-key speech that sounded at times as though he was still on the campaign trail, had to remind himself once that he was no longer leader of the opposition.
But, as he remarked, some things in Britain's tradition-bound parliament never change. One of them is the knee-jerk hostility of some Conservatives to the mere mention of the word Europe.
He mentioned the word. Two prominent Conservative Euro-sceptics, Bill Cash and Sir Michael Spicer, shot to their feet, interrupting Blair as they pleaded to be heard.
"Allow me to complete my sentence. Allow me what you never allowed the previous prime minister," Blair said witheringly.
He then indulged Spicer, who sincerely congratulated Blair on his victory and then asked him to resign if he conceded further sovereignty to Brussels at next month's European Union summit.

The prime minister shrugged off the resignation invitation and then had the last word by thanking Spicer and his fellow Euro-sceptics for contributing to Labour's landslide by exposing the Conservatives' deep divisions over Europe.
Major was also warm, genuinely so, in the congratulations he offered Blair, and promised friendly cooperation as far as possible.
But in a wry, good-humoured speech, he could not help teasing him for adopting so many of the policies that voters had so comprehensively rejected at the election.
The mood in the House was one of great expectations, with the Labour benches palpably conscious of the burden of responsibility that comes with their convincing mandate.
The colourful clothes of the 101 Labour women members of parliament, brightening up the arrays of sober men's suits, were just one sign of the far-reaching changes ushered in by the election.

And watching over it all from the visitors' gallery was the man who thought before the 1992 election that he, too, would soon be speaking as prime minister: former Labour leader Neil Kinnock's bitter-sweet emotions could only be guessed at.
